newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala left stages huge march on day of peace.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala left stages huge march on day of peace.

text.p: Thousands of Guatemalans marched in the capital on Sunday, openly declaring support for Marxist rebels for the first time in decades, hours before the signing of an historic treaty to end 36 years of war.

The government and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels prepared for the signing by calling for reconciliation among Guatemalans embittered by the brutalities that marked the war, the last of Central America's conflicts.

Students, trade unionists, visiting Salvadoran rebels, and colourfully-dressed Indian peasants from remote highland villages celebrated the end of violence in a march that stretched along one of the main streets of the capital.
They also remembered the war's victims, some 140,000 of whom died, many in mysterious circumstances.

Beneath the jubilation ran a strong current of scepticism about whether the government would be able to fulfil extensive promises for social programmes in the peace accords, and change the lives of the 80 percent of Guatemalans who live in poverty.

"There is cautious euphoria. But it is not really happiness. You can't have much happiness after 140,000 deaths," said 37-year-old Mario, who declined to give his last name out of fear of reprisals, but openly wore a guerrilla bandana.

At the height of the war in the 1980s, Guatemala's powerful army earned a reputation as the hemisphere's worst human rights thug, staging counterinsurgency campaigns that led to peasant massacres and torture and assassination of opposition leaders.

President Alvaro Arzu recently said he was not asking Guatemalans to forget such crimes. But the peace treaty includes a partial amnesty, and he called on citizens to forgive each other and look toward the future.
Rebel commanders, returning to Guatemala on Saturday for the first time after decades in exile, also called for reconciliation. They were met at the airport by hundreds of cheering supporters.

While their supporters chanted in the streets, the four members of the URNG high command, Rolando Moran, Pablo Monsanto, Carlos Gonzalez and Jorge Rosal, met in a hotel on Sunday with government counterparts to wrap up last minute details of the final peace agreement.
Their troops stayed in mountain camps to watch the signing on television.

Ten presidents from Latin America and Spain flew in over the weekend to attend the gala peace signing ceremony, which was scheduled for 5 p.m. (6 p.m. EST/2300 GMT)at the National Palace -- an imposing building that once contained an office where army intelligence masterminded persecution of leftists.

On arrival, foreign dignitaries lauded Arzu for bringing peace to Guatemala, many giving him the bulk of the credit for pushing peace talks to a conclusion less than 12 months after taking office last January.

Although the talks had stumbled along intermittently since the URNG and the government first began negotiating in 1991, Arzu gave a jolt to the process by meeting personally with the rebel commanders to express his commitment to the talks.
He also has shown himself ready to rein in the army, purging corrupt officers with unprecedented boldness.

"I am quite impressed with Arzu from a personal standpoint and (with) his vision for the country," said Thomas McLarty, White House envoy for Latin America who headed the United States delegation to the signing.

Guatemalans had hoped for a higher level U.S. delegation, including Vice President Al Gore, noting that U.S. intervention has helped shaped the country's fate, especially during the Cold War years of the 1950s to 1980s.
